ARC: The Five Principles (641)

=== EPISODE 10: Bupmin (641)
## Flowering Youth
It is the spring Bupmin turns fifteen.
The Hwarang train under the Marshal: horse, bow, verse, and above all gyuku, a horse-ball game a lazier age will call polo.
Bupmin (15) is old enough for the headband and too young to invent a country alone. His father is in the Council chamber collecting votes. His uncle keeps the yard.
[diagram hwarang]
Yushin does not soften the yard because the boy is royal. He softens nothing. The new boys sleep six to a hall and learn each other's snores before each other's ranks. They trade rumours about the Marshal like relics. He took forty fortresses. He bathes in a haunted lake. He can hear a lie drop a shoulder at fifty paces.
Girls crowd the fence of the yard the way other towns crowd a market — not for the ball, for the Hwarang. They pretend they came for the verse.
Nobody in Surabol would dream of calling gyuku a pastime — it is a ranking system with horses, and a boy’s seat among the Hwarang is half his blood and half his swing. Handicaps are argued the way ministers argue borders, only with less honesty.
Then there are the clubs. A premium gyuku club is not a stick. Third-growth cypress from the south ridge of Namsan, seasoned seven years in the shade of Hwangnyong, the grip wrapped in indigo the Queen’s seamstresses will not sell. The head travels in its own box. If you cannot name the forest, you are not asked back.
herald: That club — Gaya ironwood core? / No — Wolseong cypress. Last season’s. / …Last season? And he brought it out?
alchun: A True Bone does not play last season’s shaft. / Is that law? / Worse.
yushin: Again. / A king for all who cannot hold a saddle is a poem, not a country.
munmu: Uncle— / I said that when I was six.
yushin: Then make it true at fifteen. / The Hwarang do not train for your father’s cleverness. They train for the hour the cleverness runs out.
yushin: We ride the eastern practice roads until the Fortress of Radiance looks small behind us. / Westward, Baekje’s Yellow Mountain pass is where their grain carts complain in dry weeks — learn a landscape before it learns your name.
The Hwarang follow a set of Five Principles.
At dusk he gathers the flower youth under the eaves and speaks the Five Principles the way other houses recite ancestors — not as decoration, but as the only map that still works when bone rank fails. The boys mouth the words along with him, elbowing each other at no retreat, going quiet at no needless killing, each privately certain the Marshal is looking straight at him. He is looking at all of them.
yushin: Loyalty to the sovereign. / Filial duty to parents. / Trust among friends. / No retreat in battle. / No needless killing. / Bupmin — which one will you break first?
munmu: …Retreat. / When Gotaso rides too fast I always pull up first. Every time. / If I am to be a king for all, I cannot be the boy who only follows.
yushin: Good. / Then see the country the way a Hwarang sees a field — who holds, who falters, who dies for a vow they meant. / I am marshal of this order. You will learn loyalty here before you learn how to sit on a throne.
The yard has two names it still whispers. Tonight the Marshal says them out loud…!

=== EPISODE 11: Sadaham (641)
## The First Class
Every yard has its ghosts. This one has two, and they have never missed roll call.
The lamps go up under the eaves. Nobody sends the boys to bed. They decide this is an honour, and they are right, though not for the reason they think.
The Marshal does not let trust among friends stay a pretty line. He tells the new boys of the first class — the two names the yard still lowers its voice for.
yushin: Before your fathers were born, the first class had two. / Sadaham. Mugwan. They swore to die together. Then, the year Great Gaya fell, one of them kept the swear without asking the other.
munmu: Which one, Uncle? / Which one kept it?
yushin: Sit down and you’ll find out.
A new boy: Is this the one about the haunted lake?
yushin: No. That one’s about me.
[FLASHBACK 560 the first class]
  Back then the yard was new, and so was the idea. The king wanted boys who would ride ahead of the army and not ask why. The first year, he got a lot of them. Two of them got each other.
  Sadaham is thirteen and talks like a dare. Mugwan is thirteen too, and says less than his horse. The hall has one gap, so they share it. They argue for a month about who snores.
  sadaham: You snore. / Don’t argue. The whole hall heard you.
  mugwan: That was you.
  sadaham: …Then prove it. Stay up and listen.
  Mugwan stays up. It is the first of a great many nights he will stay up for Sadaham, and the only one either of them will find funny.
A new boy: So who snored?
yushin: Both. That is not the story.
[FLASHBACK 562 too young]
  Two summers on, Great Gaya stops paying. The king calls the war in his hall, and the hall fills up with men old enough to have opinions.
  Sadaham was fifteen when he asked to ride against Great Gaya. He asked on his knees, in front of everyone. It is the only way a boy can ask a king for anything and not be sent outside.
  jinheung: Go home. Grow a beard. / War is not a yard. Nobody hands the ball back.
  sadaham: Then I’ll ask again tomorrow.
  He does. And the day after. The old general leading the campaign once took an island by frightening it with wooden lions. He tells the king it will be quicker to bring the boy than to keep hearing him.
  jinheung: Fine. Take him. / If he dies, it was his idea. Write that down.
  mugwan: You’re going.
  sadaham: We’re going. / I told them you’re my second. Don’t make me a liar.
  mugwan: You didn’t ask me.
  sadaham: I’m asking now. / …Well?
  mugwan: …I’ll get the horses.
munmu: And the battle? Uncle, what happened at the gate?
yushin: Any old man in the market will give you the gate. He’ll get it wrong, but he’ll give it to you. / I am telling you about the rice.
[FLASHBACK 562 the prize]
  Afterward the king pays him the way kings pay: in people. Three hundred Gaya captives, roped in a line, his to keep. Sadaham walks down the line once. Then he starts cutting rope.
  mugwan: The court will say you’re showing off.
  sadaham: Then the court can have them back. / Help me with this knot.
  The land they give him instead is a strip of stones by the Alcheon that nobody wanted. The chronicle calls this virtue. Mugwan calls it typical, and holds the knot.
munmu: My father would have found a use for three hundred people.
yushin: Your father would have found a use for three hundred and one.
[FLASHBACK 563 the swear]
  That winter Mugwan catches a cough he cannot put down. Sadaham sits by the mat and counts his breathing, the way they used to count snores.
  mugwan: Go eat. You smell like a sickroom.
  sadaham: You remember what we swore.
  mugwan: We were thirteen. We also swore to marry the same girl.
  sadaham: If you die first, I will not eat. / So don’t.
  mugwan: If I die first— you already know.
  sadaham: Then neither of us is allowed to be late.
  Mugwan died of illness not long after the campaign. He did it quietly, the way he did everything, before dawn, so as not to wake anyone.
[FLASHBACK 564 seven days]
  Sadaham did not take food for seven days. The cooks left bowls by his door. The order sent its oldest men to argue with him. He thanked them, and did not eat.
  sadaham: …It’s quiet in here. Nobody snoring.
  He was seventeen. The order buried two headbands and kept the story, because a Hwarang who outlives his vow is only a boy with a nice coat.
The lamp under the eaves has burned down a finger’s width. Nobody has moved. One boy is pretending he has something in his eye, and the others are kind enough to look at the lamp.
yushin: That is friends. Not a song. / If your vow is lighter than a meal, do not wear the headband.
yushin: You will still say first class when your hair is grey. Our class. His class. / The Harmony Council is the yard with better chairs — almost every sleeve there once slept six to a hall.
munmu: Uncle. / Who would you stop eating for?
Yushin looks at the boy for a long moment. You can probably name her. He doesn’t.
yushin: …Go to bed. Gyuku at dawn.
When his sister rides too fast, Bupmin always pulls up first. Gotaso never pulls up. Not for horses. Not for anyone…!

=== EPISODE 12: Gotaso (641)
A young girl is going to do what she’s going to do.
It begins two springs earlier, with a girl who is not where she is supposed to be.
Gotaso (16) goes out to the lantern market with two maids and does not come back with any. The maids are found first, by the river, in the morning.
munhee: Husband. / …Husband.
Chunchu says nothing. This is the part the household remembers afterwards and none of them can describe properly: he does not shout, he does not ask a second question, he simply stops being the man who talks.
I did not know, then, that silence was the loudest vow I would ever make. I know it now.
yushin: Chunchu. Sit down. / I already have men out.
chunchu: …
yushin: …Chunchu.
chunchu: How many horses do we have.
It is the only sentence he speaks for two days. Yushin will try to tell it later as a joke and will stop halfway through, every time.
They were not bandits, in the sense that bandits want money. No word came and nothing was asked for, which is worse, and Chunchu understood what it meant before anyone in the room said it aloud.
They find the road on the second night. What Chunchu does at the ford is in no record, because the two men who could have written it down were at the ford.
yushin: Enough. / Chunchu. Enough. / …The child is watching.
He stops. He wipes his hands on the grass, carefully, both sides, the way a man does before he picks up something clean.
chunchu: …Gotaso.
gotaso: Father… there is something on your coat.
chunchu: So there is. / I will change it later.
He carries her the whole way home. It is nineteen li. He does not let anyone take a turn and he does not put her down to eat.
munhee: …Put her down. / Your arms will come off.
chunchu: A little longer.
yushin: I have never seen you go quiet like that.
chunchu: …Brother. / I have two sons and one daughter. / One daughter.
Before the wedding, there is a year that nobody writes down — except, privately, in the scorebooks of the spring gyuku match.
At a spring gyuku match the Hwarang ride for the Queen. The stands smell of horse and expensive varnish. Servants carry club-boxes the way other households carry ancestral tablets. Princess Gotaso (16) is only meant to watch.
munhee: Look at that club box. / Namsan cypress, Hwangnyong shade-dried. / A Hwarang that young carrying that… you can see the household.
gotaso: I am not looking at the club. / Only the man.
Pumsuk (23) takes the ball on the off-side — a showy, illegal-looking, completely legal cut — and for half a breath too long catches her eye instead of the goal. His premium gyuku club flashes once in the sun: presentation-silk still on the headcover, five coloured rings on the shaft, vulgar as Surabol sport gets.
gotaso: …Who is that. / Mother. / Mother. I asked who that is.
munhee: Hwarang Kim Pumsuk. / Don’t stare.
gotaso: I already did. / And he looked back. He did, he did.
gotaso: I am never going to look at anyone else. / For the rest of my life.
munhee: …Fifteen years old, using the word “life.”
gotaso: Fifteen is exactly when you are allowed to use it. / Later you get too embarrassed.
She looks at him the way a person looks at weather they have decided to live in — not bargaining, not counting rooms. Just the face.
They meet again under the flowering trees behind the training ground — not by accident the second time, and not the third.
Under the flowering trees they forget to be a princess and a Hwarang.
pumsuk: I shouldn’t… see Your Highness here.
gotaso: Then why do you come every day. / I come every day. / Yesterday I came twice.
pumsuk: …I don’t know. / Knowing I shouldn’t.
gotaso: And I’m not supposed to… touch your hand either? / Then why… won’t you let go of my wrist.
pumsuk: You mustn’t. / …And yet you’re holding it. / And… I cannot take it back.
Rain finds them once on the palace steps. Neither of them moves to go inside.
gotaso: You’re soaked. / …Why are you smiling. / Ah. / Is it my hair… on your sleeve?
pumsuk: Your hair is… caught on my sleeve. / I should free it. / My hand won’t move. / Neither will my feet.
gotaso: Then leave it. / Leave it there. / The sleeve. The hair. / I could stand beside this sleeve for the rest of my life. / No — closer.
pumsuk: My lady. / If this goes on… I will come apart. / Here. On the steps.
gotaso: So will I. / So I settled all of it last night. / Four children. I have named them. / I am telling my parents today.
pumsuk: …Four?
gotaso: You don’t want them?
pumsuk: …I want to know the names.
Four children, already named. Now the boy has to ask her father. And her father wants a vow…!

=== EPISODE 13: Pumsuk (641)
Princess Gotaso (16) has fallen in love with the Hwarang Pumsuk (23), and the whole court can see it before either of them admits the word. The maids keep score of the accidental meetings. The guards move their posts to give the flowering trees more privacy than any regulation requires. The entire palace is, quietly, on her side.
Her parents Chunchu (38) and Munhee (35) bless the marriage. Then, over his wife’s one quiet objection, the father asks the boy for a vow — a vow no father should make his daughter hear.
munhee: Don’t make him swear.
chunchu: …Why not.
munhee: If he keeps it, it was owed anyway. If he cannot, it kills him.
He makes him swear. It is the only time in this record that Chunchu misreads a room, and it is the room with his daughter in it.
chunchu: If anything happens to her, you know I’m going to kill you, right? Haha...
pumsuk: On my life, I will protect Lady Gotaso!
At the back of the hall, the Queen watches her niece marry for love.
[FLASHBACK 626 the girl-child]
  The girl-child arriving: again the white, again only Samsin and Munhee. Pink silk already too sure of itself in a void that has no furniture to flatter it.
  Munhee does not watch the vows. She watches the doorway and remembers a different night in the same house: the girl-child arriving, pink silk already too sure of itself, Chunchu’s hand huge around a wrist that would never learn to be still. They named her Gotaso when the lantern-band was the same shape it is tonight.
sunduk: …Your son’s girl. / That doorway has taken three of this house now.
chunmyung: Four. If Your Majesty counts honestly.
sunduk: …I count honestly.
gotaso: We will be happy forever!
pumsuk: …My lady. Your hands are cold. / But the back of your neck… is hot.
gotaso: Because I am shaking. / And… because yours are too warm. / The hand at my waist. / Don’t take it away.
pumsuk: Are you frightened? / If I… come closer.
gotaso: No. / Because I want to be somewhere with nobody in it. / Look at me once more.
Behind the doors the feast falls away.
The new couple move to Daeya Fortress, where Pumsuk has just been named Guardian. She waves from the cart until the capital is out of sight; he rides beside the wheel the whole way. Daeya is a border post. Nobody at the wedding said the word border out loud.
The hall empties. The Queen does not leave, and neither does the Marshal. Neither of them has ever been the first to leave a room.
She has had twenty years to learn the back of his neck: the place the armour strap has worn shiny, the two grey hairs at his temple that were not there before the last campaign. Tonight the hall is empty and nobody is writing anything down, so she looks at all of it.
Color rises along her throat. She keeps her mouth closed so the breath will not give her away. He does not turn. That is the only mercy left in the room.
yushin: Your Majesty.
sunduk: …Not that word. Not tonight.
yushin: Then what am I to call you.
sunduk: Don’t call me anything.
He takes one step. It is the smallest thing he does in this entire record and it costs him longer than any battle in it.
yushin: Today you watched your niece marry the man she loves. / I watched your face the entire time. / Your Majesty—
sunduk: Yushin.
yushin: …You said my name.
sunduk: So stop.
yushin: One sentence. Let me have one. / Two horses. Tonight would be enough. / Three days to the border. After three days we are nobody at all.
She reaches up. He is very still, the way a man is still when he has already decided not to be the one who moves. Her fingers find his mouth before the rest of the sentence can.
sunduk: Don’t say it. / If you say it, I have to hear it for the rest of my life.
yushin: Then hear it for the rest of your life.
For a moment she does not answer, and the moment is long enough that both of them will spend years deciding what it meant.
Her fingers are still on his mouth. He does not take the next step. The lamp between them does the looking. When she speaks again she is already Queen.
sunduk: …Without you this country does not last half a year.
yushin: You are talking about the country.
sunduk: Because the country is the only thing I am permitted to talk about.
She is close enough now to count what it is costing him. She counts it. Then she takes her hand back and puts it where a queen’s hand goes.
sunduk: One more step and I do not stop.
yushin: …Then I will not take it.
sunduk: Thank you.
yushin: Don’t thank me. / That is the sound you make when you have won.
sunduk: …Then neither of us has.
He steps back into the shape of a subject. It fits, because he has worn it twenty years. It has never once fit.
yushin: Your Majesty.
sunduk: …Yes. That will do.
Neither of them mentions that night again. Thirty-two years later, on the last day of his life, he is asked whether he ever wanted anything for himself, and the record notes only that he took some time to answer.
Outside the hall, two lantern-sellers argue the way Surabol argues anything that matters — by nickname first.
?: The Legend of the Hwarang — Bidam — still sits at one hundred and eight with the Last Son of Gaya. / And the most cunning man in Samhan packed his daughter’s wedding like a campaign. Watch the roads, not the vows.
At the feast's edge, a southern merchant named Haesang pours a story instead of wine. He has seen harbours where the ships have eyes painted on the prow. He has bought glass from men who swore it came from past the edge of every map. He never boasts. He doesn't have to.
haesang: In the south they greet a guest before they ask his rank. / I recommend it. Rank keeps. Guests leave.
haesang: Your southern wine came late. The carter blamed the Yellow Mountain road. / Then he blamed the White River mouth. Then he blamed both blades. / Every harbour tavern from Funan back has that fight — the Sword of the Divine Country, or Hundred-Victories out of the Land of the Heavenly Deer. / Nobody has ever settled it. Which is why the wine is late.
“Dear… have you already forgotten how we met?” Munhee hasn’t. It involves a dream, a skirt, and a coat torn on purpose…!

=== EPISODE 14: Munhee (625) [flashback]
## How They Met
chunchu: Dear… have you already forgotten how we met?
It starts with a dream, and the dream is sold.
bohee: Last night… I climbed Namsan and I relieved myself, / and all of Surabol drowned. / The entire capital.
munhee: Sister. Sell me that dream.
bohee: …For what?
munhee: My silk skirt.
Bohee takes the skirt. It is the single worst trade in Silla’s thousand years, and the two of them will both live long enough to know it.
munhee: The capital you drowned / is mine now.
Five days later Yushin brings a young nobleman home from the gyuku field — still dusty, still arguing about a disputed foul — and on the yard, mid-demonstration of a “proper True Bone grip,” steps on the hem of the man’s coat on purpose. The tie comes away.
yushin: Oh dear. / My apologies. / Somebody sew that for the gentleman.
bohee: …How could I approach a nobleman over so small a thing.
munhee: I will do it.
He has to take the coat off for her to mend it. Magenta silk leaves his shoulders. He sits disrobed in her brother’s hall with a True Bone’s embarrassment and nowhere to put his hands. She knits the tear standing close enough to feel the heat off his skin — and that is all, the first time. Needle. Breath. The slow fact of a man without his coat.
chunchu: …Your hands are quick. / I have… not sat like this.
munhee: Sit. / I will put the coat back on you. / Today… only that.
He comes back the next day, needing nothing sewn, and again the day after that. Each visit she finds a new place on the garment — and they sit closer. The needle slows. His breath learns the back of her hand. They do not leap. They accumulate.
On a later visit the coat is off again. She stands behind him, needle forgotten, staring at the breadth of his shoulders as if the knitting were only an excuse to keep looking. Magenta silk has slipped. She does not tell him to cover it. When the needle pauses it is because her mouth has found the place above his pulse — and Yushin is careful to be looking somewhere else the entire time.
chunchu: …Why. / At this rate… I will tear the coat myself.
munhee: Because you have not left yet. / Before you leave… / your hand belongs at my waist. / Until the sewing is done.
He comes back the next day, needing nothing sewn, and again the day after that — and each time she finds a new place on him that needs mending with her mouth.
On a later visit she stands behind him, needle forgotten, staring at the breadth of his shoulders as if the coat were only an excuse to keep looking. Magenta silk has slipped. She does not tell him to cover it.
munhee: And what is torn today? / Or… what shall I tear for you.
chunchu: …Nothing. / No — / Here. / Where your mouth… was yesterday.
munhee: Shall I tear something for you, then? / Only the coat. / Or… your restraint as well.
chunchu: …If you say it like that. / I won’t be able to leave tonight. / I am already… coming apart at the door.
munhee: Then don’t. / The sewing… can wait until morning. / Spend the night… mending me.
He stays. The household learns the sound of a door that is not meant to open until dawn.
By midsummer the household staff have stopped announcing him.
munhee: N-no, why bring up that memory again…
Yushin invites him back onto the gyuku field. Chunchu is not especially good at gyuku — his club is respectable Mid-Bone pine, which the Hwarang notice immediately — and Yushin knows it.
yushin: Pregnant, with no husband to name… what disgrace is this!
Yushin builds the pyre in the yard where they played gyuku, which is not lost on anyone, and sets green wood on it so that it smokes instead of burning.
The smoke goes straight up. It is visible from Namsan. It is visible from the terrace where a princess happens to be standing with the young nobleman who has gone the colour of paper.
sunduk: What is that smoke?
chunchu: I-it’s me!
yushin: …Chunchu. / You did not choose my sister. / I chose you.
chunchu: Brother.
yushin: Do you know how many years it took me / to lay Gaya blood and Silla royalty in the same bed.
chunchu: You should have simply become king yourself. / Surely the strongest man in Samhan ought to be the one who rules.
yushin: (laughing) Chunchu. You know exactly why not.
chunchu: …I do.
Neither of them says the word. It sits between them anyway, the way it always has: Gaya. His grandfather bought the family a rank. Ranks are not the same as blood.
sunduk: Lord… Chunchu?
chunchu: Th-the father of that child… Lady Munhee’s… I mean… / It’s me!
Chunchu   Munhee are married — the burnt-skirt rumour becomes a wedding, and the wedding becomes a household that is openly fond of itself.
## The Closed Months
The wedding itself is quiet. Magenta silk and pink silk share a cup. What the court will later call a clever match is, in the room, simply two adults who have already learned each other’s breath.
They shut the door on the yard and do not open it again for a long time. The minutes will later invent one decorous wedding night. What actually happens is weeks of it — her on him, him on her, the magenta and the pink in a heap by the door — until the meals go cold and Surabol learns to wait.
The first time he is still trying to be gentle. She is not. She takes his hand and puts it where she wants it, and the sound that leaves her is not a toast. He lasts like a man who has been polite too long, which is to say not long, and says her name at the end as if he were apologising for it. She laughs, because that was the point, and does not let him go anywhere. The bedding. The chest. The floor, when the bedding is too far away. When he reaches for the water jug she pulls him back by the wrist.
munhee: Again…? / Today… don’t even try to count. / Save counting for outside.
chunchu: I… cannot count. / Munhee. / I have… already lost. / And… I will lose again.
For weeks they do not leave the bedding except to drink, to laugh, to start again. She wakes with him still beside her and starts again before the laugh is finished. She rides him until her thighs shake and asks for more the way she would ask for a sum he is good at. A strategist who can forecast a betrayal a generation out cannot forecast his own stamina, and does not care.
The neighbors on both walls learn their names the wrong way — through plaster, through 다시, through a rhythm that does not stop when the lamp does. Servants stop knocking. Someone on the east side moves a sleeping mat farther from the shared timber and blames the draft.
At night the courtyard looks up and learns worse. The paper window glows — warm lamp inside, blue-black street outside — and on the 창호지 the shadows are unmistakable: one figure straddling the other; two bodies pressed to the lattice; upright, tangled, a lift that makes a silhouette into a confession. No faces needed. The pose is the gossip.
A neighbor freezes mid-step under the eaves, looks up at the shadow on the lattice, and looks away too late. By the third night half the lane has an opinion, and none of it is about politics.
munhee: They say… they heard us through the wall. / And saw… the paper window. / Even our names.
chunchu: Then the wall… is on our side. / And the paper window. / If Surabol hears… / let it.
They fit. Not the polite fit of a well-arranged marriage: when he is all the way with her she makes a noise like someone who has been waiting years for exactly that, and then laughs into it, because he is already moving again. Neither pretends to be shy. Later the household will call it love, which is also true. In the bed she only says again, and don’t you dare stop.
Morning finds them still tangled — lattice light on flushed faces, her thigh over his hip, the pink silk she never put back on crumpled under them. He wants her again before he is properly awake. She laughs into his mouth and lets him, slowly this time, which is somehow worse. He kisses the place above her pulse the way she once kissed his. The strategist’s cleverness has nowhere to go but her.
munhee: Dear. / Outside… later. / For now, count only me.
chunchu: That… / is the one sum I am good at.
Months pass before either of them remembers the yard. When they finally open the door she walks like someone who has been thoroughly loved and does not mind the lane knowing it, and they look at each other like people who have won a private war — still in love, still hungry, and willing, for one afternoon, to put clothes back on.
When they reappear, the marriage is already a fact the city has stopped gossiping about — replaced by the quieter envy of people who heard the walls, saw the glowing lattice, and wished their own houses were that lucky.
## Bupmin’s Birth
Samsin is there the way she is always there when a breath starts — and no one else. Pitch white. Mother and midwife. The rest of the house can wait outside the light.
Years later the same house keeps a different quiet. Munhee holds the boy against her collarbone. They will call him Bupmin. The lantern makes a low band of light across the bedding and leaves the rest of the rooms uncounted. Chunchu sits where a husband sits when he has not yet learned what the child will steal from him.
The household fills with Bupmin, who walks early, and Gotaso, who talks early and never stops.
After that, Chunchu stopped going to the hill.
yushin: You have not been coming to Council lately.
chunchu: Brother. I have two sons and a daughter now. / The east star… I think I will let it just be a star.
yushin: So you will.
In Surabol, one father puts down his star. In Pyongyang, another marches his son to school without taking off his boots…!

=== EPISODE 15: Grand Academy (641)
Yeon's wife has given him three sons. They could not be more different.
Namseng (7) is the careful one — the heir, eager to be approved of.
Namgun (4) is the fierce one, who never backs down first.
Namsan (2) is the quiet one, watching his brothers.
There is a fourth boy at that table who is not counted, because counting him would require a word nobody in the house wants to use. Gulgul eats after the others and says nothing, and Namsan — who watches everything — is the only one who notices that he never sits with his back to a door.
## The Taehak
The Grand Academy is old. It came over the river in the same season as the first Buddhas. Ever since, the school and the temple have shared Goguryeo's noble sons. Classics in the morning. Sutras after lunch. Archery whenever the masters lose their voices.
Yeon brings Namseng (7) to the gate himself, in riding boots, and does not take them off on the swept stone.
Taehak Master: Commander. The sons of the five commanderies begin with the Analects and the Lotus Sutra. / As your own father did, if I remember the register.
gesomun: The Analects, fine. A boy should know how to bow before he decides not to. / The sutra he can skip.
namseng: Father. / Is the Buddha not allowed?
gesomun: The Buddha’s fine. Fat, quiet, never asked me for anything. / It’s his landlords I mind.
The landlords are not a figure of speech. Half the good valley land belongs to monasteries. The monasteries belong to the great houses whose second sons run them. None of it pays for the wall. Every spring Yeon writes to the Summit about this. Every spring the Summit thanks him for his piety.
What he wants instead is the Way of Laozi, which is an odd thing for him to want, because the Tang emperors claim Laozi as their ancestor. Yeon has heard this and does not care. He has a sentence for it, the only one he ever repeats word for word.
gesomun: A pot stands on three legs. / Confucius is one. The Buddha’s two. We’re missing the third, and the pot’s tipping into the fire.
Taehak Master: The third leg would be… Tang priests, Commander?
gesomun: The third leg is whatever doesn’t own a farm.
Across the courtyard a monk named Bodeok has stopped sweeping. He is from the monastery at Banryong, which owns a great deal of farm, and he will remember the sentence longer than anyone else who hears it.
The complaint reaches the High Commander’s table before Yeon has ridden home. Gusesa reads it at supper, between courses.
gusesa: (mild, wiping his fingers) A Yeon telling monks what to own. / My nephew collects enemies the way other men collect horses. At least horses eat less.
Namseng is enrolled anyway. He learns the Analects first and best, and on the days the sutra master is ill he reads his father’s copy of the Daodejing, which has never been opened past the first page.
Field trip. Yeon takes the boys to see a very big rock. The rock has a list on it, and a question…!

=== EPISODE 16: Stele (641)
Yeon takes his sons to see the Great King's stone. It lists everything he ever took.
namseng: Aw… that’s it? A big rock?
Every Goguryeo boy is raised on him. He kept the west shut, and he made it look easy.
gesomun: Sixty-four fortresses are written on that rock. / When you can read, you will read them to me. / …And then you can ask how a country that took sixty-four came to bow to Chang’an twice a year.
Late in the year, old Dosuryu walks in without taking off his boots. In thirty years he has never once done that…!

=== EPISODE 17: Dosuryu (641)
Late in the year Dosuryu comes in without knocking, which he has done since Gesomun was small enough to lift by the collar, and without taking his boots off, which he has never done.
gesomun: Oi. Old man. Boots.
dosuryu: Shut up and sit down. / No — stay standing. You listen better standing.
dosuryu: His Majesty and your uncle. Three times this month, the same little room behind the audience hall. / Nobody else in it. Not even a boy to pour.
gesomun: So they drink together. Good for them.
dosuryu: They don’t drink. That’s what’s wrong with it. / Ever since you walked out of the Summit, your name comes up in that room. They mean to send you to the far end of the wall in the spring. And have you not come back from it.
gesomun: HAHAHAHAHAHA
gesomun: Kill me? Yeon Gesomun?
dosuryu: Laugh. Go on. / Your father laughed at the Summit for twelve years and came home grey. You haven’t got twelve years. You’ve got till spring.
Yeon stops laughing. He does it all at once, the way a door shuts.
gesomun: How many names on their list.
dosuryu: One that I know of. Yours. / …Why are you smiling like that? Stop it. I hate it when you do that.
gesomun: Then I’ll make a list too. / Mine’ll be longer.
Dosuryu goes out the way he came in, boots and all, and stands a long time in the yard before he can make himself mount. He has known the boy for thirty years. He knows exactly what kind of list it will be.
Meanwhile in Sabi, Euija is king at last. On his coronation morning, several hundred people see a dragon…!

=== EPISODE 18: King Euija (641)
King Mu is dead at eighty, after a lifetime of fighting Silla.
Euija takes the throne at forty-one. The court will style him Righteous and Merciful. He has a sense of humour about that.
On the morning of his coronation a dragon is seen over the Sabi River. Several hundred people see it. The court diarist writes it down, because it happened.
It was four lacquered paper kites, a low mist, six boatmen paid in advance, and one hour of the year when the light comes up the river at exactly the right angle. Euija had been planning it since the previous autumn.
gyebek: …Your Majesty. That is not a dragon.
euija: No, it isn’t. / Now go and say so to those people standing there. / See who wins.
gyebek: Wins what. / It is paper and sticks. I can see the string. / I will go and tell them. You said to.
euija: They cannot see the string. / I did not say go. I said see who wins.
gyebek: That is the same order. / I will not call it a dragon anywhere.
euija: Stand here for one hour. Mouth shut. / You cannot do the other thing. That is why I keep you beside me.
courtmaid: Your Majesty. We saw the dragon too. / …From beside you.
euija: …You two know better.
courtmaid: We do. / But of all Your Majesty has made… the thing that lasts longest isn’t a dragon.
euija: …What did you say.
courtmaid: Miracles, Your Majesty. / The kind you keep close only at night.
His father had done it first, and better. Before he was king, King Mu paid the children of Sabi to sing a song he had written himself. By the third month the song was older than anyone could remember, and what it said about him had become a thing everybody had always known.
Nobody had to pay the children again. Euija filed that away.
euija: The thirtieth Eraha bought a country with a song. No army, almost no money. / I was twelve. Nothing since has impressed me that much.
So the reign begins with small wonders. All of them arranged. None of them expensive.
The white deer is the cheapest one. You take a young doe, you keep it out of the sun for a season, and you let it out on the hunting ground on a day the ministers are watching.
The stone at the Rock of Politics sweats before a good decision. It sweats because somebody rubs it with brine the night before, and the somebody is always the same man.
Rice comes up on ground where nothing was planted. Something was planted. It was planted at night.
seongchung: Your Majesty. What happens when the people work it out?
euija: They won’t. / Nobody inspects the evidence for a thing they already want to believe.
He walks the riverbank the morning after the dragon as if the mist itself had appointed him. Children point. A grandmother weeps. A clerk from the Board of Rites drops his brush and does not pick it up, because picking it up would mean deciding whether to write what he saw or what he was told.
euija: Look at them. / An army takes a month to move a border. / A story moves it overnight, and thanks you for the privilege.
gyebek: Your Majesty is… enjoying this.
euija: I am good at it. / A man should enjoy what he is good at. Otherwise he does it badly, out of spite.
At the Rock of Politics he arrives last, lets the ministers wait, rests two fingers on the sweating stone as if taking a pulse, and smiles the small smile of a physician who already wrote the prescription.
euija: The rock agrees. / How fortunate for all of us that the rock has such good taste.
gyebek: The rock did not agree. / It is brine. I can smell it. / I am not going to nod at a wet rock.
euija: The ministers are listening to the rock. Not to you. / Do not nod. Silence they can misread. Your mouth they cannot.
euija: Gods are props. Spirits are lighting. / And any man who believes it is already in my cast.
seongchung: …Your Majesty.
euija: Seongchung. Hate the method. You have my permission. / Only do not stand there telling me it does not work.
courtmaid: Tonight? / One miracle, or two?
euija: Two. / I am in a generous mood. / The country can watch the dragon. You can watch the king.
This is the Righteous and Merciful at full height: before the wine years. He wrote the sky this morning. He walks under it and does not look up.
This is entirely correct, and it is the sentence that kills him, nineteen years later, word for word.
Two court maids attend him — close enough that the air between them feels arranged. He is proud of the number the way a man is proud of a hunger he has not yet failed to satisfy.
He does not count faces. He counts the hem — how far the long chima rides when she pours, whether the stair takes the silk to the thigh.
euija: Two is enough. / One is lonely, and three… the room grows small. / And when it is small… hands forget where they belong.
courtmaid: Your Majesty. / Which of us sits beside you today? / Or… shall both of us only share your breath.
courtmaid: With Your Majesty’s wrist… between our knees.
euija: …Don’t both be greedy. / I am… looking at a map.
courtmaid: The greed is Your Majesty’s. / You look at us… as if you already know. / Our throats… are closer than the map.
euija: …I was talking about the Silla border.
courtmaid: Yes, Your Majesty. / Your voice is at its best when you talk about borders. / So we keep asking.
courtmaid: If you say our names… in that voice, / the ties… come undone first.
euija: …Leave.
courtmaid: Shall we? / Your Majesty has not let go.
nation-baekje: Righteous and merciful — so he was named. / Land of the Heavenly Deer, Land of the Lord Buddha — keep both names warm. One is for merchants. One is for monks.
Gyebek is twenty-one. No market calls him Hundred-Victories. Not yet. He is passed over every season, because nobody knows what clan he comes from, and he won't make one up.
## The Princes
At the coronation feast the princes sit by age, and the table has to be lengthened twice. Yung sits nearest the king, with a Satek cup-bearer at his elbow. Behind every brother's chair stands a clan tutor, like a second shadow. At the far end, servants pour for boys who don't have names worth carving yet.
euija: Look at that table! The thirtieth Eraha left me a country. I made a second one out of sons. / Count them, Seongchung. Go on. I lose track after thirty.
seongchung: Forty-one, Majesty. If the two born this spring are counted. / …And each of them will need a chair, one day. There are only so many chairs, and—
euija: Then we’ll build more chairs. Or empty some. / Pung! Where’s Pung?
Prince Pung (17) stands. He is the quiet one, the one with the good handwriting, and he already knows what is coming because his mother told him the night before, crying into his collar.
euija: The East wants a prince of Baekje at its court, to show the world how close we are. You’re going. / Learn their poems. Drink their wine. Don’t marry anyone I’ll have to go to war over.
pung: As Your Majesty commands. / …For how long?
euija: Until I need you. / Ha! Don’t look like that. It’s a compliment. Nobody sends a prince he doesn’t mean to want back.
One day Baekje will send for him after all. Nobody at the feast would have believed it, Pung least of all.
Euija can fake a dragon. He can’t fake a fortress. For that he needs a general who does exactly what he says…!

=== EPISODE 19: Yunchung (641)
There was only one man Euija knew he could trust to deliver.
That winter Euija sends for Yunchung, and nobody from the eight houses is told. Yunchung is a general from a family too small to keep a clan tutor. He has held the Silla frontier for eleven years by doing exactly what he says he will do, which the Assembly finds tiring.
euija: Sit, General. No, the good cushion. Take it before I change my mind. / Tell me. Who rules Baekje?
yunchung: Your Majesty does. / On paper.
euija: Ha! And off paper?
yunchung: Off paper, the Rock does. And whoever rubs the brine on it. / The eight houses pick the Premier, the Premier picks the ministers, and the ministers send me the grain late. They pay my men. My men know it.
euija: So. How does a king get his country back off the Rock without a war at home?
yunchung: With a war abroad, Majesty. / A king who wins a fortress owns the men who took it. The clans can’t vote on a victory. They can only show up to the feast.
euija: Plainly put. / I like a man who says the ugly thing without a cushion under it. Even when he’s sitting on mine.
It is the first time in the reign that Euija says what he has decided before the Assembly hears it. By spring the Assembly will hear it anyway, in the form of a question he has already answered.
That winter, the Assembly's loud fight isn't about war. It's about a shipping writ. A Satek cousin has died without a son, and somebody has to inherit the salt, the iron and the run to the islands. Gyebek sits through three sessions. He understands every number and none of the smiles.
ministersatek: The writ stays in the house. / A harbour that changes clans mid-monsoon is how grain rots in the hold.
elderyunbi: Then say clan, not country. / We are tired of hearing harbour when you mean Satek.
euija: Enough. / When the frontier is settled, you may resume counting berths. / Until then — the Eraha counts fortresses.
Euija has already decided. Now the clans have to believe it was their idea.
The Premier is chosen via the Rock of Politics — a ritual the Great Clans have controlled for generations.
[diagram ministers-assembly]
chunbok: As Your Majesty well knows, / the will of the Rock is the will of Heaven. / The eight houses decide it together.
euija: Heaven…? Ah — the invisible committee. / Spirits and gods — the cheapest civil servants. / They never ask for berths, they never read the ledger, and the people kneel without being told twice.
nation-baekje: Restore the reign of the thirteenth Eraha…! / The thirteenth Eraha…! Ten thousand years!
euija: Ah… in Silla, they worship the Cloud King like a god. / Do you know what kind of man the Cloud King was…?
euija: He signed an alliance with us, and then he took the river. / Surabol carved him four stones for it.
euija: Do you know what a country is? / A country is a territory governed by a single story. / Why are we Baekje people, and not Goryeo or Silla people? We look exactly the same. / Anywhere in Baekje, everyone knows the founders. / Speak of King Onjo — that is Baekje. / So the king makes the story. / Let us make an interesting one…!
euija: Goryeo is too large to move. / Silla is too old to surprise anybody.
chunbok: The present king of Silla is a woman who cannot command an army, / and even within her country, the people’s hearts are unsettled. / Seize this opening, take a border fortress, and the great work will be within reach.
seongchung: Your Majesty — is this the country you mean to hand the princes?
euija: No, Gyebek… not you. / Why use an ox-cleaver to kill a chicken?
gyebek: Your Majesty. Does that mean you will not use me, or that you are saving me?
euija: …It means I am saving you.
gyebek: Then say that. I do not follow figures of speech.
The Assembly finds him rude, which misses the point by a courtyard’s width. All he wants — every single time — is the sentence handed over with nothing folded inside it, and nobody at that court has spoken that way in their lives.
euija: A border fortress… / That too is good. / Daeya… how about it?
euija: In truth… the people of this country need a new story. / They have lived in the old one long enough.
euija: There was a time we were the greatest power in Samhan. / The thirteenth. He led armies into the heart of Pyongyang. / Then came the Severing. / After that, Baekje was a fraction. The name stayed. The size did not. / And then heaven, helpful as always, sent signs. A new king, meant to save us. / The thirty-first. Great King Euija.
gyebek: What is the Severing.
euija: You said you do not follow figures of speech. / This is not one. It is the Severing. / Today we only have to tell it.
euija: Baekje… is in crisis! / Then we make the crisis.
euija: We take back the Silla frontier.
yunchung: Then we’re done for, plain and simple.
euija: Ha! Then go and be done for at Daeya, General. Ten thousand men. / Bring me back the fortress. And a story to go with it.
yunchung: Daeya by autumn, Majesty.
“What is the Severing?” Gyebek asked. Any grandmother in Sabi could tell him. We’ll go back a hundred years and see for ourselves…!

=== EPISODE 20: The Severing (553–554) [flashback]
The sad thing about betrayal… is that it never comes from your enemies.
Two kings take a river back together. One is Seong of Baekje. The other is the Cloud King. The deal is simple. Baekje gets the river mouth, near the sea. Silla gets the upper valley.
For a while the two banners still fly side by side. Then the Cloud King turns his army on Baekje's half. He takes the river mouth and gives it a new name. He fills it with men who won't ask what the alliance meant.
King Seong feels the cut in the marrow. He calls in everyone who still owes him: the last Gaya houses, a boatload of soldiers from the islands. Then he marches on the fortress that opens Silla's throat.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 19, Emperor Kinmei, yr. 15 (554), 12th month; Aston tr., vol. 2, pp. 72–73 · cf. Samguk Sagi bk. 4, Jinheung yr. 15] King Seong of Baekje, with troops of Gaya and Wa, attacked Gwansanseong.
For months the fight goes Baekje's way. The crown prince holds the forward camp, half-starved. One night his father rides out with fifty horse to steady him.
Silla’s ambush is waiting. The road to the prince is a ditch that was not there at dusk. Fifty horse stop, because the torches coming up the bank are the wrong color.
On the ridge, Jinheung’s hand drops. That is the signal. He has already said the rest, low, to the only man the rank will allow to finish it.
jinheung: You. A slave. / He is a lord with a name. / A slave does the cutting. So later mouths cannot forget it.
A man in a Gaya cone helm is already down in the cut. He wears Silla's commission over it. His cone cuts the night ridge. He does not draw. He watches.
kingsung: Gaya…? / A prince of Geumgwan — on this road, tonight, why.
muryuk: Military governor of Sinju. / Sit.
They sit him on a camp stool. Out of the cone’s shadow a man kneels twice, the way you kneel to a king, and asks.
dodo: …I’m asking. / Let me take the head.
kingsung: What. / A slave’s hand— no. A king’s head does not take a slave’s hand.
dodo: If you broke the oath. / Even a king… takes it. I was told.
muryuk: Dodo.
kingsung: Every time I think of it… / It went into the marrow. / I cannot live on in disgrace.
He looks up. The breath that leaves him is not another sentence. He unfastens his own knife, gives it to the kneeling man, and puts his neck out.
The ditch takes the head. Dodo does the work the rank will not put on a prince’s hands. The record almost forgets the slave. Silla keeps the skull under the steps of the north hall, names the hall the capital court, and sends the rest of the bones home.
[QUOTE Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 19, Emperor Kinmei, yr. 15 (554), 12th month — the killing of King Seong (明王); Aston tr., vol. 2] Silla told Kodo, a horse-tending slave of Sajichon, renamed Gokji: Kodo is a low slave and King Seong a lord with a name; have the slave kill the lord, so later ages will hear it and not forget it in the mouth. Kodo captured the king, bowed twice, and said, Let me cut off the king’s head. The king answered, A king’s head should not receive a slave’s hand. Kodo said, By our law, if one breaks a sworn alliance, even a king receives a slave’s hand. The king sat on a camp stool, unfastened his own sword, and gave it to Gokji to cut with. He looked up to heaven, sighed loud, wept, and consented: Whenever I think of it, the pain has always reached the marrow. Reckoning it, I cannot live on in disgrace. Then he stretched out his neck and received the cut. Kodo cut off the head and killed him. Silla kept the skull and sent the rest of the bones to Baekje with rite. The Silla king buried the bone under the steps of the north hall, and named that hall the capital court.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 26, Baekje Annals — King Seong, yr. 32 (554), 7th month] In the thirty-second year, autumn, the seventh month, the king wished to raid Silla. He personally led fifty foot and horse and came by night to Gucheon. Silla’s ambush rose. They fought, and he was killed by the disordered troops.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 4, Silla Annals — King Jinheung, yr. 15 (554); cf. bk. 26 note] The subordinate commander, Godo Dodo of Samnyeonsan commandery, struck at once and killed the king of Baekje.
Baekje’s court never forgives the cloud that emptied itself over their side of the river. A hundred years later, when Euija tells the story, he is still telling this one.
Back to now. Ten thousand Baekje men march on Daeya. Its grain clerk is called Gumil. Remember that name…!
